Over breakfast, the crew argued about what a pop song was really about and whether waitresses deserved a tip at all. Bram cut the debate short, handing out the tree aliases for the heist, though Mr. Birch immediately objected to being named Mr. Birch.

When the store alarm tripped, the robbery collapsed within a minute. Mr. Ash shot his way clear of the police from the getaway car with Mr. Elm beside him. Fleeing on foot after they were separated, Mr. Elm hijacked a car and was shot in the stomach by the terrified driver, whom he shot dead in return. Mr. Ash found him, driving the screaming Elm to the warehouse rendezvous, cradling his bleeding head and swearing he was not going to die.

Weeks before the bleeding, undercover officer Danny Roarke had rehearsed a fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet with his handler Pruitt. They ran the lie over and over until Danny could tell it like an absolute memory.

Inside the quiet warehouse, Mr. Birch arrived, bleeding from his own close call. He argued heatedly that the job was a setup with an informer inside it, then slipped outside to hide the diamonds beyond the perimeter. 

Danny had performed that exact toilet anecdote for the boss Bram, his son Cal, and Mr. Ash, earning their trust until Bram took him onto the crew as Mr. Elm. That same week, Ren Vasco walked out of prison after years inside and reported straight to Bram and Cal, who owed him everything for the long years he had kept his mouth shut.

Mr. Cedar strolled casually into the warehouse and produced a kidnapped patrolman, Doyle, from the boot of his car. Left alone with the bound officer while Birch paced outside, Mr. Cedar turned on a radio oldie, danced to the music, cut off Doyle’s ear, and doused the screaming man in petrol. From his place on the floor, Mr. Elm raised his revolver, shot Mr. Cedar dead, and whispered to Doyle that he was a cop and that the police were already waiting outside for Bram.

Cal returned moments later, listened to Elm’s breathless account of Cedar’s madness, and casually shot Doyle dead himself. 

Finally, Bram arrived. He ignored the bodies and pointed directly at the wounded man on the floor, naming Mr. Elm as the informer who had sold them out. Mr. Ash refused to believe his boss, raising his gun and turning it directly on Bram. The sudden three-way standoff erupted into gunfire, leaving Bram, Cal, and Ash all shot, with only Ash and Elm still breathing among the ruins of the crew.

Bleeding out, Elm looked up at his protector and confessed that he really was a police officer. Ash stared at him in disbelief, raising his weapon and shooting Elm just as the tactical police units stormed the warehouse, cutting Ash down in a hail of gunfire.

Hitmen Rollo and Marcus drive across the city, debating foreign drug laws and what fast food is called abroad. Waiting in the corridor outside their target’s flat, the two argue over whether a foot massage is worth killing a man for. Upon entering, Marcus recites a passage of scripture before the pair shoot a young man named Tobin for double-crossing their employer, Otis, successfully recovering a leather briefcase. Suddenly, a fourth man hidden in the bathroom empties a revolver at them without hitting either, an impossible miss that Marcus insists is divine intervention. In the getaway car afterwards, Rollo’s gun accidentally goes off and blows the head off their passenger Del. Marcus parks the bloodied car at his friend Warren’s house, where a sharp fixer directs the cleanup and provides the men with fresh clothes. Later, over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decide on the spot to hold up the diner they are sitting in. Marcus calmly talks the robber down mid-holdup, hands over his own wallet, keeps the briefcase, and lets the couple walk out. The two hitmen finally deliver the briefcase to Otis at his bar, where Otis is busy paying the ageing boxer Denny to take a dive in the fifth.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war delivers to a young boy the gold watch his father kept hidden through years of brutal captivity. Decades later, that same boy—now the fighter Denny—double-crosses Otis, wins the fight, kills his opponent in the ring, and escapes in a taxi. While hiding in a motel with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny discovers she has left his father’s watch behind in his flat. Risking his life, Denny returns for the watch and shoots Rollo dead with a submachine gun left sitting on the kitchen counter.

Rollo buys heroin from his dealer Kip and shoots up before his night out. He takes Otis’s wife Nadia to a themed diner where they win the dance contest. The evening turns disastrous when Nadia snorts Rollo’s heroin, overdoses, and is barely revived by a violent adrenaline shot to the heart on the dealer’s living-room floor.

Leaving his flat after the shooting, Denny and Otis collide in the street, crash, and are taken prisoner in the basement of a pawnshop. Denny breaks free, comes back with a sword pulled from the shop wall while one of their captors is raping Otis, and slays the attacker. Otis declares them square on the condition that Denny leaves town immediately. Denny collects Marielle and rides out of the city on a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop.

An immigrant shopkeeper named Nadir stood in the gun store with his daughter, Sahar, enduring the dealer’s cruel mockery of his accent as they purchased a heavy black handgun. That same evening outside a downtown restaurant, Trey and Kwame ambushed prosecutor Halstead and carjacked his luxury sedan. On patrol nearby, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay and Renee Hobart, groped Renee in full view of her humiliated husband, and released them with a smirk and a warning. Disgusted by the encounter, Boyle’s partner, Voss, went straight to their commander to request a new patrol car rather than spend another shift riding alongside an unrepentant racist. 

The next morning, locksmith Mateo arrived at the Halstead residence to change the locks. As he worked, Paula Halstead stood nearby, loudly insisting to anyone listening that he was a gang member who would undoubtedly sell duplicate keys to criminals. Mateo moved on to his next job at Nadir’s shop, replacing the deadbolt and warning the owner that the wooden door frame itself was severely compromised. Angered by the added expense, Nadir accused Mateo of pulling a dishonest con. 

Across town, Boyle stood pleading before a health insurance clerk named Delia Frank, begging for coverage for his dying father, only to be coldly refused. 

Months in the future, Renee Hobart would find herself trapped upside down inside a burning automobile, choking on smoke until Officer Boyle—the very officer who had assaulted her on the night of the traffic stop—crawled through the flames to drag her broken body to safety.

That night in the present, Nadir’s shop was smashed open and looted down to the bare walls. When the insurer arrived, they refused to pay a single cent because Nadir had ignored Mateo’s warning about the compromised door. 

Desperate to escape the law, Trey and Kwame sped through the dark, running down a shopkeeper named Pham before dumping his battered body outside a hospital emergency room. Soon after, Clay Hobart attempted to recover his stolen vehicle, only to be caught mid-carjacking by arriving police; Voss intervened, successfully talking the other officers out of shooting Clay on the spot. Clay seized the wheel, drove Trey away from the swarm of squad cars at high speed, and shoved him violently out onto the pavement.

Driven mad by ruin, Nadir waited outside Mateo’s home with his hidden handgun. As Mateo stepped onto the porch, his small daughter Rosie ran squealing into his arms, and Nadir pulled the trigger. The child was untouched; Sahar had secretly loaded the gun with blanks, and as the echo faded, Nadir collapsed, weeping in the belief that the girl was his saving angel.

Iterating through his shift, Voss picked up Kwame hitchhiking along a dark strip of road. When Kwame reached into his jacket pocket, Voss panicked, misread the gesture, shot him dead, and set the car ablaze to cover the crime. Detective Isaiah Reece was called to the roadside scene the following morning, pulling back the sheet to discover the charred victim was his brother Kwame. At home, their mother berated Isaiah, blaming him bitterly for never once going to look for his lost brother.

In her suburban home, Paula Halstead tripped at the top of her staircase and tumbled to the bottom; bruised and weeping, she grabbed her housekeeper Alba’s hand, sobbing that Alba was the only friend she had left in the world. 

Meanwhile, Trey discovered Pham’s abandoned delivery van packed with frightened, trafficked migrants. Rather than selling them to local handlers, he drove them straight to the harbor docks and set them free. 

As the first snow of the year began to blanket the city, two cars slid across the icy pavement, colliding softly and sparking yet another vicious argument in the street.

The newsreel obituary finished playing in the dark projection room, recapping Emmett Rusk’s grand public life but closing without explaining his mysterious last word. Sent by his editor to discover what "Bluebell" meant, the reporter Nash tracked down Emmett’s second wife, Nora, at a seaside nightclub, but the drunk former singer rudely turned him away at the door. 

Nash retreated to the vast, cold halls of Silvermount to begin his research, opening the published memoir of the late banker Barrow. 

In its pages, Nash read how Emmett’s story had begun out west in a dreary mining boarding house, where Emmett’s mother signed her son over to Barrow after a defaulted lodger’s mine deed unexpectedly made the family rich. The outraged boy had driven his sled straight into Barrow’s stomach, but he was taken east away from his parents anyway. Years later, on his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett took full control of his fortune and informed Barrow that of all his vast holdings, he wanted only to run a failing city newspaper called the Clarion. Emmett moved into the Clarion’s building, installed his manager Marsh alongside his friend Devlin, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. To consolidate his power, he hired away the entire staff of a rival paper and celebrated with a grand party featuring a brass band and a chorus line.

Setting the memoir aside, Nash sought out Marsh and later located Devlin, listening as the men recounted Emmett’s middle years. 

They remembered when Emmett returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. A run of tense breakfast-table scenes soon charted that high-society marriage cooling into absolute silence behind separate newspapers. Seeking solace, Emmett met a shopgirl named Nora Kell on the street with mud splattered on his coat, and he soon started visiting her rooms in secret. Mid-campaign during Emmett's own run for governor, political party boss Halloran brought Adele directly to Nora's apartment and threatened public exposure, but Emmett stubbornly refused to withdraw. Emmett subsequently lost the election, a disillusioned Devlin asked to be transferred to another city, and the marriage to Adele collapsed completely. 

Emmett married Nora and promptly forced her into an opera career for which she possessed no voice whatsoever. Nora’s opening night debut was a total humiliation; a drunk Devlin began a savage review of her performance, which Emmett finished himself, printed in the paper, and then fired Devlin for. Tobias spent hours boxing up every object connected with Ivy so the technicians could map the attached memories. Ivy had already hired the memory-erasure clinic to remove every trace of Tobias from her mind. Her choice followed the night she came home drunk having dented Tobias's car, triggering a fierce argument that ended with her walking out for good—the tragic end to a relationship that had slowly curdled into bitter recrimination over Ivy's drinking and Tobias's emotional withholding.

Insurance investigator Martin Kray interviewed Elias Prine, ruling the man’s sudden memory loss psychosomatic and denying his claim. Soon after, Prine’s diabetic wife tested her husband by asking for repeated injections, dying of the overdose he could never remember administering.

In a derelict basement, Martin beat and strangled the drug dealer Gil Marsh, snapping a photograph of the body. As life drained from him, Gil whispered a single word—“Elias”—which Martin could not explain before changing into the dead man’s suit and speeding away in his sports car.

The true turning point came when intruders attacked Martin and his wife in their bathroom; though Martin killed one, a heavy blow to the head robbed him of the ability to form new memories. To hunt the surviving attacker known only as R.M., he constructed an elaborate system of instant photos, annotated notes, and permanent tattoos.

Plainclothes officer Roy met him outside, revealing that Gil was innocent, that Martin had already killed his wife’s true attacker a year prior, and that Martin himself was the tragic protagonist of the Prine case. Refusing to accept the revelation, Martin burned the pictures of Gil, scrawled *he is lying to you* across Roy’s photograph, copied down the officer’s license plate, and drove to a parlor to have the digits inked on his thigh as his sixth unshakeable fact.

A year before, Roy had quietly helped Martin find and execute the real culprit, a vengeance Martin forgot within minutes. Now trapped in an endless reset, Martin sat in an unfamiliar motel room, reciting the Prine investigation over the telephone to an anonymous caller.

Stepping into a local bar clad in Gil’s clothes, Martin ordered a beer that the staff, recognizing their boss’s gear, promptly spat in. The owner, Corinne, hid every pen in her house to exploit his condition, goaded him into striking her, and blamed a rival named Vance; driven by her deception, Martin ambushed Vance in a motel bathroom, beating him viciously before driving him out of town at gunpoint.

Standing alone in a desolate field, Martin burned his late wife’s hairbrush and books, attempting to grieve a loss his damaged brain could never retain. Moments later, the anonymous telephone caller fed him a name and a location, pointing him toward Gil Marsh.

Corinne ran Roy’s license plate through an insider at the vehicle registry and handed Martin the official record identifying Roy Mercer. Guided by the paper, Martin lured Roy back to the derelict building, shot the officer cleanly through the head, and photographed the corpse to forever seal the truth.

Helicopters sprayed the city for crop pests through the night, their dull blades thrumming endlessly over every neighborhood. Beneath that steady hum, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, quietly got ready for a dinner party. Elsewhere in town, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake for a young boy named Charlie Rill. 

The next morning brought a sudden violence when Charlie was knocked down by a car driven by a waitress named Rhona on his way to school. Though shaken, the boy walked home insisting he was fine, but later that day he collapsed into a deep coma. His parents, Grant and Elaine, kept a desperate vigil at his bedside in the hospital. As the hours stretched on, Grant's estranged father Duff turned up at the hospital and unburdened himself, confessing an affair from decades ago. Meanwhile, back at the shop, unpaid and entirely ignored, the baker grew bitter and started making anonymous menacing phone calls to the grieving family.

Across town, telephone-sex worker Cheryl talked men through their explicit fantasies from her living room while her husband Stu seethed in silence beside her. Seeking an escape, Stu and three friends drove out to fish, only to find a young woman's body floating face down in the river. Rather than packing up immediately, the men tethered the corpse to the muddy bank and carried on fishing for two more days before finally telling anyone. When they returned, Vern's wife Iris, who worked as a party clown, was utterly disgusted when she learned what the men had done.

In a quiet flat overlooking the darkened avenue, an old man gestured toward the glass and explained to a younger man that nothing survives time.

Below that window, police officer spotlights flashed against the wet pavement as officers handcuffed Cort and Jonah, dragging the shouting pair out of the club and onto the street.

Just moments earlier, deep inside the dark venue, Jonah had lifted a heavy fire extinguisher and beaten a man’s face into a red ruin, entirely unaware that the real criminal, the pimp known as the Adder, watched the brutal spectacle from only a few feet away.

Cort’s arm had already been snapped with a sickening crack after he had hunted wildly through the crowded club and seized that same innocent stranger, mistaking him for the monster who had hurt Lise.

Outside in the alley before entering, two sketchy men had approached Cort and Jonah, offering to sell them the rapist's real name and steering them directly toward the flashing neon sign of the club called the Pit.

Before that desperate hunt began, Cort and Jonah had stumbled out of the warm house party into the cool night air, stopping dead in their tracks as they watched paramedics load a battered, unconscious Lise into the back of an ambulance.

She lay bleeding because the Adder had trapped her in the shadows, raping her and savagely slamming her head against the cold concrete while a lone passer-by caught a brief, terrifying glimpse of the assault and backed away into the darkness.

Lise had only ended up in that subterranean hell because she had chosen to take the pedestrian underpass rather than cross a roaring, busy road, stepping straight into a nightmare where she caught the Adder violently beating a transsexual woman.

She had been walking through the night alone because Cort had spent the evening getting steadily drunk and high, openly pursuing other women until a disgusted Lise turned her back on him and left the party.

Hours before the argument, the night had begun with laughter as Lise, Cort, and Jonah rode the underground together toward the gathering, cheerfully arguing about sex and ribbing Cort about his heavy drinking.

Earlier that afternoon, the world had seemed peaceful and bright as Lise sat reading a novel in the park, listening to the gentle hiss of water sprinklers and the laughter of playing children while one hand rested softly against her stomach.

Before going to the park, she had stood entirely alone in the quiet flat, staring down in stunned silence at the small plastic stick of a pregnancy test, watching the two bold lines form to reveal that it was positive.

And earlier still, before any test or terror, Lise lay tangled in the bedsheets beside Cort, lazily describing a strange recurring dream she had about a long red tunnel while the two of them teased each other playfully about her ex-boyfriend Jonah.

As a product-recall investigator driven mad by insomnia, I found that the only thing that let me sleep was crying at support groups for diseases I did not have. Then Ada Vey started attending the same groups, and her obvious faking destroyed my release. Searching for an escape, I took a business flight where I met a soap salesman named Rex Marrow and pocketed his card. When my flat and all my catalogue furniture were destroyed in a sudden explosion, I called Rex, who took me into a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district. Outside a bar one night, Rex asked me to hit him as hard as I could, and the two of us beat each other bloody in the car park.

Years later—or so it felt in the flash of a waking nightmare—I would stand high in a tower, a bullet hole torn through my cheek where I had placed a gun in my own mouth to destroy Rex. Ada Vey would be brought to me by shaven men, her fingers laced in mine at the window as we watched the debt-record towers collapse into dust.

In the car park, what started as two men brawling soon hardened into a weekly basement club with its own strict rules, pulling in more and more members every night. The chaos deepened when Ada overdosed; Rex brought her back to the derelict house, and the two of them began a loud, agonizing affair I could not stand. Rex’s side projects grew stranger still: he rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into luxury soap, selling it back to high-end department stores at eighty dollars a bar. During one ritual in the kitchen, Rex burned my hand with chemical lye and held me fast, refusing to let me retreat into meditation while the flesh scorched. 

Using my raw, beaten face as terrifying evidence, I blackmailed my employer into paying me a full salary to simply stay away from the office. Freed from work, Rex turned the basement club into a radical organization he called Havoc, filling our derelict house with obedient, shaven recruits who took orders and vandalized corporate property across the city. The madness escalated until Rex deliberately steered our car into oncoming traffic, let it roll violently, and then vanished into the night. 

When a member of Havoc named Ogden was shot dead on an operation, guilt seized me, and I started travelling to try to shut the whole thing down. Moving from city to city, I was stunned to find identical basement clubs everywhere, populated by men who greeted me respectfully as Rex Marrow. 

In the quiet terror of a hotel room, I finally worked out the truth: I and Rex were the exact same person, and Rex had been taking over my body to act while I slept. I tracked down Ada, who confirmed the truth—she had been sleeping with me all along, not with a separate man. 

Terrified of what my alternate self had planned, I discovered that Havoc had mined the towers of the major debt-record companies with explosives, and I rushed into the complex to defuse the charges. Inside the dark structure, Rex materialized to stop me, brutally beating me down a concrete stairwell in one of the towers. Realizing the only way to banish him forever was to end my own mind, I put a gun into my mouth and shot myself through the cheek, killing Rex in the blast. 

Bleeding and breathless, I stumbled to the top floor just as Ada was delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits. Standing together in the ruin, we held hands at the window as the surrounding debt towers came crumbling down into the dark.

Emlyn sat in his friend’s armchair that evening, watching Wilder unravel. He explained calmly that he had known about the affair for four full years, ever since his wife had told him during their journey abroad. He added, with a cold, even smile, that he had never thought particularly highly of Wilder’s letters either.

Wilder had rung him earlier in a state of absolute panic, begging him to come over at once, and Emlyn had complied without hesitation. 

Only hours before, Odile had let slip to Wilder that Emlyn was publishing a particular contemporary writer—one whom Wilder represented, though both men quietly detested him. 

They had been sitting in a bar, two years after the end of their secret domesticity, when Odile first shattered the evening. She had told Wilder then that her marriage was finally over, admitting that she had spent the previous night confessing every detail of their past to her husband.

Before that final unraveling, there had been the quiet dissolution of their secret life. Deciding at last that the rented rooms had become an exhausting chore, Wilder and Odile had carefully split the crockery between them and surrendered the lease.

Yet the friendship between the men had dragged on in strange, suffocating patterns. Over dinner at the married couple’s house, Emlyn and Wilder had spent the entire evening discussing racquet games and old schoolboy sports, driving the conversation so relentlessly that Odile had no part in the talk at all.

Days before that dinner, Emlyn had drunk his way through a long, heavy restaurant lunch with Wilder. Throughout the meal, Emlyn had baited the agent endlessly about contemporary fiction, taunting his professional taste while never once mentioning the betrayal he had learned of.

Odile had only just returned to the rented rooms after the journey abroad. She had said nothing whatever about the trip or what had transpired, and the afternoon had passed in quiet routine, exactly as all the others had before it.

The confession itself had happened thousands of miles away. In a hotel room abroad, after her husband noticed a letter held for her at the front desk addressed in a hand he instantly recognized, Odile had confessed the truth. Emlyn had listened, then remarked casually that he had always been far fonder of his friend than of his wife.

Before that trip, in the peaceful sanctuary of their secret flat, Odile had broken delicate news of her own. She told Wilder she was carrying her husband’s child. After a quiet pause, the pair had decided that the rented rooms would go on exactly as before.

It had taken work to establish that quiet life. Months earlier, Wilder and Odile had rented the set of rooms in a quiet district, filling the cupboards with fresh linen and matching plates to give their affair a proper household of its own.

And long before the rooms, the linen, or the long years of deceit, there had been a party at the house of Emlyn, Wilder’s closest friend. While the other guests drank and laughed downstairs, a young book agent named Wilder had led Odile up the stairs to a quiet room, taking her hand to tell her just how lovely she was.

A beam weapon flashes, killing him instantly in front of a silent crowd he has just finished addressing. He has always known this is how it ends.

In a glass-walled zoo on a distant world, he sits beside a famous film actress while alien onlookers observe them. The creatures explain to him that every moment in time exists simultaneously, and that free will is merely a delusion unique to his own planet.

A weak, peculiar child sinks straight to the bottom of the deep end, thrown into the water by a father intent on teaching him to swim. He was born in a bleak industrial town where no one expects much of him.

He marries the daughter of the man who owns the local optometry school, an alliance that quickly makes him immensely wealthy.

Lost behind enemy lines, he lies in the frozen mud, begging to be left to die, until the scout with him delivers a severe beating to force him to his feet.

A host adjusts a microphone in a broadcast studio while he speaks on a late-night radio talk show, attempting to explain the fourth dimension and the nature of the aliens to an unbelieving audience.

In a hospital ward where he lands after collapsing upon his return from abroad, a neighboring patient introduces him to a hack science fiction writer.

In the prisoner-of-war camp, he observes the neighboring barracks, where a long-standing clerical error allows enemy officers to draw double rations year after year.

His daughter sits in an office, signing legal papers that strip him of his affairs, convinced that his mind has surrendered to senility.

On a crowded prison train, the captured scout’s leg turns black with gangrene. With his final breath, the dying man blames him for their capture and ruin.

Another prisoner leans close in the shadows of the barracks and promises that, in time, he will see him killed to avenge the scout.

Drafted into the army and given no training worth mentioning, he is sent overseas to serve as a chaplain’s assistant.

A charter plane smashes into a snow-covered mountain slope, and he walks away from the wreckage unharmed. Miles away, his wife drives frantically toward the hospital to reach him, only to die in her car, asphyxiated by leaking exhaust fumes.

He is housed with other captives in a disused abattoir inside a great city. One night, a tempest of fire consumes the entire metropolis. Safe within the thick walls of a subterranean meat locker, the prisoners survive, stepping out the next morning to find the city entirely erased.

Under the eye of guards, the survivors spend days excavating corpses from buried cellars, shoveling soot and ash until one of the diggers retches violently and dies of the dry heaves.

Dressed as devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew robbed a diamond house in a northern port, walking out with a massive, priceless stone. Far overseas, his cousin Marv called with urgent instructions: Solly needed to bring the diamond straight over to him. Before Solly could leave, Grigor the Nail told him about a busy bookmaker’s shop in the city—and simultaneously tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to ambush Solly at that very location.

Meanwhile, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their prized fighter, Pretty Sam, to buy a caravan from a nearby camp of travellers. The transaction soured when a tough bare-knuckle fighter named Finn knocked Sam unconscious over the deal, leaving Halloway without a contender for the gang boss Coldstone’s upcoming fixed bout. Desperate for a replacement, Halloway was forced to put Finn into the ring instead, promising Coldstone that Finn would take a dive in the fourth round.

Solly landed in the city, delivered the diamond to a fence named Hersch, and immediately headed for the bookmaker’s to bet on the fight. At the shop, Ike, Benno, and their accomplice Tulley utterly bungled the planned robbery; in the frantic melee, they severed Solly’s arm and snatched his briefcase before Grigor chased them off. That evening, Finn ignored his instructions and knocked his opponent out cold in the very first round. Coldstone lost a fortune on the result and brutally took out his frustration on Halloway.

Marv flew into the city, discovered Solly was gone, and hired the ruthless bounty hunter Ledge to track him down. Shortly after, Grigor captured Solly himself and cut off his remaining arm to force open the stolen briefcase, only to discover that the diamond was not inside it. Ledge quickly traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces, and took both the men and the recovered stone into his possession. Coldstone then fed Solly to his hungry pigs and grimly warned Halloway and Digby about what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong.

Halloway and Digby strictly instructed Finn to go down in the fourth round of the rematch. To guarantee his compliance, Coldstone’s heavy-handed men torched the travellers' camp, burning Finn’s mother to death inside her caravan.

Before the fight took place, Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car while Ike and Benno were trapped inside. A bloody street battle erupted, and in the shootout, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. Amid the violent chaos, Tulley escaped into the night with a dog that had swallowed the priceless diamond.

Halloway and Digby strictly instructed Finn to go down in the fourth round of the rematch. To guarantee his compliance, Coldstone’s heavy-handed men torched the travellers' camp, burning Finn’s mother to death inside her caravan.

Before the fight took place, Grigor ambushed Ledge’s car while Ike and Benno were trapped inside. A bloody street battle erupted, and in the shootout, Ledge, Grigor, and Benno were all killed. Amid the violent chaos, Tulley escaped into the night with a dog that had swallowed the priceless diamond.
